summary.title: Just use Postgres
summary.one_liner: Ethan McCue argues that Postgres should be the default database for new applications with persistent data, and walks through why alternatives like SQLite, DynamoDB-style NoSQL, Valkey, Datomic, XTDB, Kafka, ElasticSearch, and commercial databases usually don't fit better.
keywords: kafka vs postgres append only log
elasticsearch vs postgres full text search
takeaways: Default to Postgres for new applications that need persistent storage, unless you have a specific reason not to.
SQLite stores data in one file, so it suits single-machine desktop or mobile apps better than multi-server web apps that need network-accessed databases.
DynamoDB-style NoSQL databases (Cassandra, MongoDB) need access patterns and queries designed up-front; relational databases are more flexible.

Newer or experimental databases (Datomic, XTDB) and proprietary ones (Oracle, MSSQL) carry risks of lock-in, limited support, or ecosystem gaps; Kafka, Elasticsearch and Valkey are specialized tools for specific needs.
summary.summary: The author gives opinionated advice: use Postgres as the default for new applications needing persistent storage. He explains the trade-offs of SQLite (single file, single machine), DynamoDB, Cassandra and MongoDB (up-front access pattern design, weak ad hoc querying), Valkey as a primary database (RAM limits), Datomic and XTDB (niche language support, newness), Kafka (Postgres tables work as append-only logs at small scale), ElasticSearch (only when search is the core product), and commercial databases like Oracle and MSSQL (lock-in cost). He ends by admitting he is unsure how MySQL compares to Postgres and asks the audience for input.
